title: Accountability Final Rules: The Reprieve Is Real, but So Is the Risk
author: Phil Hill
summary: Phil Hill takes stock of the U.S. Department of Education's newly finalized institutional accountability rules, which for the first time put a broad program-level earnings test at the center of Title IV eligibility for nearly all academic programs. His central framing is that the timeline changed but the substance did not: the effective dates have been pushed back — the program participation agreement language takes effect around September 2026, the accountability machinery for most programs on July 1, 2027, and tipped occupations such as cosmetology not until July 1, 2029 — yet every flaw of the Earnings Premium concept survived the comment period intact. Hill walks through the six-step cadence by which a metric travels from program completion to consequence (always looking several years into the past), notes that the rule's six-digit CIP6 basis means institutions will be 'blind for an additional year' on program-level results, and argues the real shift is that program review is now a matter of institutional risk belonging with presidents and boards, not a routine academic exercise delegated to deans.
points: For the first time, the federal government is putting a broad program-level earnings test at the center of Title IV eligibility for nearly all academic programs.
The reprieve is about timing, not substance: effective dates are staggered — PPA language around September 2026, most programs July 1, 2027, and tipped occupations July 1, 2029.
Nothing changed in the underlying Earnings Premium concept — earnings measured four years after completion against survey-based thresholds — despite commenter pushback that ED rejected.
Because the rule runs on six-digit CIP6 codes while visible datasets are CIP4, institutions will be 'blind for an additional year' on what the framework does to specific programs.
The real shift is that program review becomes a matter of institutional risk belonging with presidents and boards, not a routine academic exercise delegated to deans.
quotes: For the first time, the federal government is putting a broad program-level earnings test at the center of Title IV eligibility—broad as in for nearly all academic programs.
In essence the effective date has been pushed back, but not by a single amount and not for everyone at once.
None of this is current; the metric is always looking several years into the past.
We will be blind for an additional year on what the CIP6 framework actually does to specific programs.
Every flaw I have described in the Earnings Premium is now a fact of life (and, I am sure, the subject of future lawsuits).
This is a new era of institutional risk, and most institutions' governance hasn't caught up to it.
